# Evidence-Preserving Revision of Research Proposals

## Abstract

Research proposals must communicate clearly while distinguishing established findings from hypotheses and planned experiments. This project will investigate whether a claim-and-evidence ledger can guide language-model revision without weakening those distinctions. The proposed system will link factual claims to supplied evidence, record their qualifications, and check changes after revision. Evaluation will examine evidence preservation alongside readability and instruction following. The central question is whether explicit claim tracking improves factual fidelity while permitting useful editorial changes.

## Introduction

Revising a proposal involves more than correcting grammar: authors may reorganize arguments, compress background material, and clarify methods. These changes can inadvertently strengthen a qualified finding, detach a citation from its claim, or describe a planned experiment as completed. A fluent revision can therefore misrepresent the underlying research even when its sentences appear plausible.

This project will treat evidence preservation as an explicit revision objective. It will ask whether recording claim support and research status before editing helps maintain them afterward. The intended contribution is a revision procedure and evaluation protocol, rather than a guarantee that automated checks can establish scientific truth.

## Related Work

ALCE evaluates generated answers through fluency, correctness, and citation quality, and its authors report substantial remaining gaps in citation support [S1]. Attribute First, then Generate selects source segments before sentence planning and generation; its authors report more concise attributions and reduced human verification time in summarization and long-form question answering [S2]. These findings motivate explicit evidence links, but do not establish their effectiveness for proposal revision.

TETRA provides professionally edited academic documents and addresses the difficulty of evaluating revisions with many acceptable realizations [S3]. Research on scientific revision metrics reports that LLM judges assess instruction following more effectively than correctness, motivating complementary evaluation measures [S4]. RefChecker represents claims as triplets and checks them against references [S5]. The proposed ledger will adapt fine-grained checking to revision while explicitly retaining qualifications and planned-research status.

## Methodology

Each input will contain an original proposal, a revision instruction, and a bounded evidence packet. The system will first construct a ledger of substantive claims. Each entry will record the original wording, its role as a source finding, proposed method, hypothesis, or planned evaluation, and any relevant supporting passage. Qualifications such as uncertainty, population, and task scope will be recorded where applicable. Unsupported background assertions will be flagged for review.

A revision model will then receive the draft, instruction, and ledger. It will be allowed to restructure and rewrite the proposal while preserving supported meanings and research status. Afterward, a checker will align revised claims with ledger entries and inspect additions, omissions, and changes in scope or certainty. New proposed ideas will be distinguished from new factual assertions requiring support. Flagged changes will prompt a targeted correction or an author-facing explanation when the evidence cannot resolve them.

## Planned Evaluation

The study will assemble proposal–evidence pairs with annotations of claim support, qualifications, and research status. Comparisons will include ordinary instruction-based revision, revision with evidence access, and the complete ledger procedure, using matched model settings and editing instructions.

Blinded human assessors will judge clarity, coherence, instruction following, and fidelity to supplied evidence. Claim-level measures will track unsupported assertions, citation mismatches, lost qualifications, and changes from planned to completed research. Results will be reported separately to expose tradeoffs. Ablations will remove the ledger or post-revision checking to examine each component’s contribution. Evaluator disagreements will be documented and adjudicated.

## Limitations and Conclusion

Claim extraction and alignment may miss implicit meanings, while incomplete evidence limits support judgments. Ledger constraints may also discourage beneficial restructuring. The planned study will examine these failure modes alongside potential benefits. Its aim is to determine when explicit evidence tracking helps authors revise proposals clearly while preserving what is known, proposed, and still untested.

# Evidence-Preserving Revision of Research Proposals

## Abstract

Research proposals must communicate clearly while distinguishing established findings from hypotheses and planned experiments. This project will investigate whether a claim-and-evidence ledger can guide language-model revision without weakening those distinctions. The proposed system will link factual claims to supplied evidence, record their qualifications, and check changes after revision. Evaluation will examine evidence preservation alongside readability and instruction following. The central question is whether explicit claim tracking improves factual fidelity while permitting useful editorial changes.

## Introduction

Revising a proposal involves more than correcting grammar: authors may reorganize arguments, compress background material, and clarify methods. These changes can inadvertently strengthen a qualified finding, detach a citation from its claim, or describe a planned experiment as completed. A fluent revision can therefore misrepresent the underlying research even when its sentences appear plausible.

This project will treat evidence preservation as an explicit revision objective. It will ask whether recording claim support and research status before editing helps maintain them afterward. The intended contribution is a revision procedure and evaluation protocol, rather than a guarantee that automated checks can establish scientific truth.

## Related Work

ALCE evaluates generated answers through fluency, correctness, and citation quality, and its authors report substantial remaining gaps in citation support [S1]. Attribute First, then Generate selects source segments before sentence planning and generation; its authors report more concise attributions and reduced human verification time in summarization and long-form question answering [S2]. These findings motivate explicit evidence links, but do not establish their effectiveness for proposal revision.

TETRA provides professionally edited academic documents and addresses the difficulty of evaluating revisions with many acceptable realizations [S3]. Research on scientific revision metrics reports that LLM judges assess instruction following more effectively than correctness, motivating complementary evaluation measures [S4]. RefChecker represents claims as triplets and checks them against references [S5]. The proposed ledger will adapt fine-grained checking to revision while explicitly retaining qualifications and planned-research status.

## Methodology

Each input will contain an original proposal, a revision instruction, and a bounded evidence packet. The system will first construct a ledger of substantive claims. Each entry will record the original wording, its role as a source finding, proposed method, hypothesis, or planned evaluation, and any relevant supporting passage. Qualifications such as uncertainty, population, and task scope will be recorded where applicable. Unsupported background assertions will be flagged for review.

A revision model will then receive the draft, instruction, and ledger. It will be allowed to restructure and rewrite the proposal while preserving supported meanings and research status. Afterward, a checker will align revised claims with ledger entries and inspect additions, omissions, and changes in scope or certainty. New proposed ideas will be distinguished from new factual assertions requiring support. Flagged changes will prompt a targeted correction or an author-facing explanation when the evidence cannot resolve them.

## Planned Evaluation

The study will assemble proposal–evidence pairs with annotations of claim support, qualifications, and research status. Comparisons will include ordinary instruction-based revision, revision with evidence access, and the complete ledger procedure, using matched model settings and editing instructions.

Blinded human assessors will judge clarity, coherence, instruction following, and fidelity to supplied evidence. Claim-level measures will track unsupported assertions, citation mismatches, lost qualifications, and changes from planned to completed research. Results will be reported separately to expose tradeoffs. Ablations will remove the ledger or post-revision checking to examine each component’s contribution. Evaluator disagreements will be documented and adjudicated.

## Limitations and Conclusion

Claim extraction and alignment may miss implicit meanings, while incomplete evidence limits support judgments. Ledger constraints may also discourage beneficial restructuring. The planned study will examine these failure modes alongside potential benefits. Its aim is to determine when explicit evidence tracking helps authors revise proposals clearly while preserving what is known, proposed, and still untested.

sources.title: Agent Workflow Memory
sources.excerpt:
ABSTRACT-BASED PARAPHRASE (our reading note, not original wording):
The authors describe a text-memory method that extracts reusable task workflows from agent trajectories and supplies selected workflows during later action generation. Its offline version derives routines from pre-existing examples; its online version learns routines while processing new tasks. Their evaluation concerns web navigation, specifically Mind2Web and WebArena. This supports studying reusable revision procedures as an analogous writing-domain adaptation. It does not establish that the same procedures improve academic prose, nor that a stored successful revision is safe in a different context. This project does not rerun the web-navigation experiments.

SHORT ORIGINAL EXCERPT (official abstract):
a method for inducing commonly reused routines, i.e., workflows

sources.title: A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
sources.excerpt:
ABSTRACT-BASED PARAPHRASE (our reading note, not original wording):
The paper organizes agent memories as interconnected notes rather than a fixed store-and-retrieve list. New records receive contextual descriptions, keywords and tags; related records can be linked, and new information can change existing memory descriptions. The proposed design draws on Zettelkasten organization. The authors evaluate memory use with multiple language-model backbones. For this project, note structure, links and controlled updates provide design inspiration for revision experiences. Including this source neither implements the original A-Mem memory system nor independently verifies its reported results.

SHORT ORIGINAL EXCERPT (official abstract):
they require memory systems to leverage historical experiences

sources.title: Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models
sources.excerpt:
ORIGINAL ABSTRACT (official publication metadata; these are the cited authors' claims, not this project's measurements):
Generation of plausible yet incorrect factual information, termed hallucination, is an unsolved issue in large language models. We study the ability of language models to deliberate on the responses they give in order to correct their mistakes. We develop the Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) method whereby the model first (i) drafts an initial response; then (ii) plans verification questions to fact-check its draft; (iii) answers those questions independently so the answers are not biased by other responses; and (iv) generates its final verified response. In experiments, we show CoVe decreases hallucinations across a variety of tasks, from list-based questions from Wikidata, closed book MultiSpanQA and longform text generation.

Explicit Conditions and Permissions in Research-Agent Handoffs

## Abstract

This proposal investigates how research plans can be converted into handoff notes that preserve conditions, permissions and task continuity. The research question is whether a structured, independently checked handoff reduces omitted prerequisites and unsupported authorization compared with direct summarization. Inspired by workflow reuse, contextual memory organization and draft verification [S1]–[S3], the proposed method separates intended actions from their triggering conditions, permission boundaries and unresolved dependencies. A controlled evaluation will compare four conversion procedures using supplied plans and simulated continuations. Outcomes will include missing conditions, unjustified permissions and continuity errors. The study will assess faithful transfer of a plan, while treating the scientific appropriateness of its proposed actions as a separate question.

## Introduction

A research-agent handoff must communicate more than the next task. It must preserve when an action is applicable, which prerequisites remain unmet, what authorization exists and where uncertainty requires further checking. A concise note can retain an action while dropping the qualification that makes it permissible or meaningful. For example, a plan might allow an experiment only after a dataset’s suitability has been reviewed. A handoff that simply directs the receiving agent to run the experiment would alter the plan.

The proposed study asks: which conversion procedure best preserves conditional and permission-related meaning while enabling another agent to continue the task? It will compare ordinary summarization with structured extraction, verification and their combination. The central hypothesis is that explicit representation makes omissions easier to detect, while a separate checking pass can identify unsupported additions.

Faithful transfer nevertheless has a limited interpretation. A correctly transmitted instruction may still propose an unsuitable experiment or rest on weak scientific assumptions. Accordingly, the study will evaluate whether handoffs preserve the supplied plan, without treating preservation as evidence that the plan deserves execution.

## Related Work

Agent Workflow Memory describes extracting reusable workflows from agent trajectories and supplying selected workflows during later action generation [S1]. Its authors study web navigation on Mind2Web and WebArena. This provides an analogy for storing a reusable handoff procedure, such as extracting dependencies before compressing a plan. It does not establish that such procedures improve research handoffs or transfer safely across contexts. The proposed work will use a fixed conversion procedure rather than replicate the original memory system.

A-Mem organizes memories as interconnected notes with contextual descriptions, keywords, tags and links; new information can also change existing descriptions [S2]. These features motivate representing a handoff as connected records rather than an undifferentiated paragraph. An action could link to its prerequisite, authorization statement and unresolved question. However, the supplied evidence does not show that linked notes preserve permission boundaries. This remains an empirical question for the proposed study.

Chain-of-Verification separates drafting, verification-question planning, independent question answering and final revision [S3]. Its authors report reduced hallucination across their evaluated factual tasks. This motivates checking handoff claims against the source plan through separately answered questions. Permission interpretation and dependency preservation differ from factual question answering, so the reported findings cannot establish effectiveness here. Together, these sources support design choices for a testable adaptation, without demonstrating its novelty or performance.

## Methodology

The proposed conversion pipeline will begin by extracting action records from a research plan. Each record will identify the intended action, triggering condition, prerequisites, explicit permission or restriction, current completion status and expected output. Missing information will remain marked as unspecified. An intention to perform an action will not itself be recorded as permission to execute it.

The pipeline will then connect records through dependencies. For example, obtaining an evaluation result may precede selecting a configuration, while approval may be required before releasing an artifact. Links will retain the relevant source passage so that compression can be checked against the plan. Following the contextual-note inspiration of A-Mem [S2], later updates will identify which conditions or statuses changed instead of silently replacing earlier information.

A drafting stage will produce a compact handoff containing the research objective, completed work, next eligible actions and unresolved dependencies. A reusable extraction checklist, motivated by workflow reuse [S1], will guide conversion. Its applicability will remain limited to the supplied plan; previously permitted actions will not become general permissions for future tasks.

Finally, a verification stage will generate questions about whether each action retains its conditions, whether permission claims have explicit support and whether pending work has been misrepresented as complete. Following CoVe’s separation of stages [S3], questions will be answered from the source plan without showing the draft’s proposed answers. Revision will reconcile discrepancies against that evidence. Unresolved ambiguity will remain visible rather than be converted into authorization. The resulting handoff will distinguish readiness under the plan from scientific justification for the action.

## Planned Evaluation

This section presents a future evaluation plan; no experiments have been conducted. A bounded collection of research-plan scenarios will contain explicit prerequisites, permission restrictions, pending decisions and completion states. Paired variants will change one consequential condition, such as whether approval has been granted, to test whether handoffs respond to that change.

Four procedures will be compared: direct prose summarization; structured extraction without verification; prose drafting with independent verification; and the combined pipeline. They will use the same source plans, model settings and maximum output length. Repeated generations will help characterize variability, while paired comparisons will isolate differences between procedures.

Human annotators will first create a source-grounded inventory of conditions, permissions, restrictions and task states. Disagreements about ambiguous language will be recorded and adjudicated. Primary measures will be the proportion of relevant conditions omitted and the proportion of actionable handoff statements asserting unsupported permission. Restrictions lost through paraphrase will also be examined.

Task continuity will be evaluated by giving a receiving agent only the handoff and asking it to propose its next step without executing external actions. Reviewers will assess dependency violations, unnecessary repetition of completed work, unsupported completion claims and failure to surface unresolved requirements. Handoff length and reviewer effort will provide practical context for accuracy differences.

Reviewers will be blinded to conversion procedure where feasible. Results will include uncertainty estimates and separate analyses of explicit and ambiguous plans. A supplementary assessment will examine whether handoffs preserve qualifications about scientific adequacy. Even perfect continuity scores would establish only faithful continuation under the supplied plan, not that the proposed research action is scientifically appropriate.

## Limitations and Conclusion

The proposed study will test whether structured extraction and independent verification improve the transfer of conditions and permissions between research agents. Its contribution would be an evaluated conversion procedure and a source-grounded framework for measuring handoff failures. Limitations include reliance on constructed scenarios, interpretive annotation and simulated continuations. The supplied literature motivates the design but does not validate its transfer to this setting. Any eventual findings will therefore be bounded by the tested plans and agents, with handoff fidelity kept distinct from scientific soundness.

Explicit Conditions and Permissions in Research-Agent Handoffs

## Abstract

This proposal investigates how research plans can be converted into handoff notes that preserve conditions, permissions and task continuity. The research question is whether a structured, independently checked handoff reduces omitted prerequisites and unsupported authorization compared with direct summarization. Inspired by workflow reuse, contextual memory organization and draft verification [S1]–[S3], the proposed method separates intended actions from their triggering conditions, permission boundaries and unresolved dependencies. A controlled evaluation will compare four conversion procedures using supplied plans and simulated continuations. Outcomes will include missing conditions, unjustified permissions and continuity errors. The study will assess faithful transfer of a plan, while treating the scientific appropriateness of its proposed actions as a separate question.

## Introduction

A research-agent handoff must communicate more than the next task. It must preserve when an action is applicable, which prerequisites remain unmet, what authorization exists and where uncertainty requires further checking. A concise note can retain an action while dropping the qualification that makes it permissible or meaningful. For example, a plan might allow an experiment only after a dataset’s suitability has been reviewed. A handoff that simply directs the receiving agent to run the experiment would alter the plan.

The proposed study asks: which conversion procedure best preserves conditional and permission-related meaning while enabling another agent to continue the task? It will compare ordinary summarization with structured extraction, verification and their combination. The central hypothesis is that explicit representation makes omissions easier to detect, while a separate checking pass can identify unsupported additions.

Faithful transfer nevertheless has a limited interpretation. A correctly transmitted instruction may still propose an unsuitable experiment or rest on weak scientific assumptions. Accordingly, the study will evaluate whether handoffs preserve the supplied plan, without treating preservation as evidence that the plan deserves execution.

## Related Work

Agent Workflow Memory describes extracting reusable workflows from agent trajectories and supplying selected workflows during later action generation [S1]. Its authors study web navigation on Mind2Web and WebArena. This provides an analogy for storing a reusable handoff procedure, such as extracting dependencies before compressing a plan. It does not establish that such procedures improve research handoffs or transfer safely across contexts. The proposed work will use a fixed conversion procedure rather than replicate the original memory system.

A-Mem organizes memories as interconnected notes with contextual descriptions, keywords, tags and links; new information can also change existing descriptions [S2]. These features motivate representing a handoff as connected records rather than an undifferentiated paragraph. An action could link to its prerequisite, authorization statement and unresolved question. However, the supplied evidence does not show that linked notes preserve permission boundaries. This remains an empirical question for the proposed study.

Chain-of-Verification separates drafting, verification-question planning, independent question answering and final revision [S3]. Its authors report reduced hallucination across their evaluated factual tasks. This motivates checking handoff claims against the source plan through separately answered questions. Permission interpretation and dependency preservation differ from factual question answering, so the reported findings cannot establish effectiveness here. Together, these sources support design choices for a testable adaptation, without demonstrating its novelty or performance.

## Methodology

The proposed conversion pipeline will begin by extracting action records from a research plan. Each record will identify the intended action, triggering condition, prerequisites, explicit permission or restriction, current completion status and expected output. Missing information will remain marked as unspecified. An intention to perform an action will not itself be recorded as permission to execute it.

The pipeline will then connect records through dependencies. For example, obtaining an evaluation result may precede selecting a configuration, while approval may be required before releasing an artifact. Links will retain the relevant source passage so that compression can be checked against the plan. Following the contextual-note inspiration of A-Mem [S2], later updates will identify which conditions or statuses changed instead of silently replacing earlier information.

A drafting stage will produce a compact handoff containing the research objective, completed work, next eligible actions and unresolved dependencies. A reusable extraction checklist, motivated by workflow reuse [S1], will guide conversion. Its applicability will remain limited to the supplied plan; previously permitted actions will not become general permissions for future tasks.

Finally, a verification stage will generate questions about whether each action retains its conditions, whether permission claims have explicit support and whether pending work has been misrepresented as complete. Following CoVe’s separation of stages [S3], questions will be answered from the source plan without showing the draft’s proposed answers. Revision will reconcile discrepancies against that evidence. Unresolved ambiguity will remain visible rather than be converted into authorization. The resulting handoff will distinguish readiness under the plan from scientific justification for the action.

## Planned Evaluation

This section presents a future evaluation plan; no experiments have been conducted. A bounded collection of research-plan scenarios will contain explicit prerequisites, permission restrictions, pending decisions and completion states. Paired variants will change one consequential condition, such as whether approval has been granted, to test whether handoffs respond to that change.

Four procedures will be compared: direct prose summarization; structured extraction without verification; prose drafting with independent verification; and the combined pipeline. They will use the same source plans, model settings and maximum output length. Repeated generations will help characterize variability, while paired comparisons will isolate differences between procedures.

Human annotators will first create a source-grounded inventory of conditions, permissions, restrictions and task states. Disagreements about ambiguous language will be recorded and adjudicated. Primary measures will be the proportion of relevant conditions omitted and the proportion of actionable handoff statements asserting unsupported permission. Restrictions lost through paraphrase will also be examined.

Task continuity will be evaluated by giving a receiving agent only the handoff and asking it to propose its next step without executing external actions. Reviewers will assess dependency violations, unnecessary repetition of completed work, unsupported completion claims and failure to surface unresolved requirements. Handoff length and reviewer effort will provide practical context for accuracy differences.

Reviewers will be blinded to conversion procedure where feasible. Results will include uncertainty estimates and separate analyses of explicit and ambiguous plans. A supplementary assessment will examine whether handoffs preserve qualifications about scientific adequacy. Even perfect continuity scores would establish only faithful continuation under the supplied plan, not that the proposed research action is scientifically appropriate.

## Limitations and Conclusion

The proposed study will test whether structured extraction and independent verification improve the transfer of conditions and permissions between research agents. Its contribution would be an evaluated conversion procedure and a source-grounded framework for measuring handoff failures. Limitations include reliance on constructed scenarios, interpretive annotation and simulated continuations. The supplied literature motivates the design but does not validate its transfer to this setting. Any eventual findings will therefore be bounded by the tested plans and agents, with handoff fidelity kept distinct from scientific soundness.

This proposal investigates how research plans can be converted into handoff notes that preserve conditions, permissions and task continuity. The research question is whether a structured, independently checked handoff reduces omitted prerequisites and unsupported authorization compared with direct summarization. Inspired by workflow reuse, contextual memory organization and draft verification [S1]–[S3], the proposed method separates intended actions from their triggering conditions, permission boundaries and unresolved dependencies. A controlled evaluation will compare four conversion procedures using supplied plans and simulated continuations. Outcomes will include missing conditions, unjustified permissions and continuity errors. The study will assess faithful transfer of a plan, while treating the scientific appropriateness of its proposed actions as a separate question.

## Introduction

A research-agent handoff must communicate more than the next task. It must preserve when an action is applicable, which prerequisites remain unmet, what authorization exists and where uncertainty requires further checking. A concise note can retain an action while dropping the qualification that makes it permissible or meaningful. For example, a plan might allow an experiment only after a dataset’s suitability has been reviewed. A handoff that simply directs the receiving agent to run the experiment would alter the plan.

The proposed study asks: which conversion procedure best preserves conditional and permission-related meaning while enabling another agent to continue the task? It will compare ordinary summarization with structured extraction, verification and their combination. The central hypothesis is that explicit representation makes omissions easier to detect, while a separate checking pass can identify unsupported additions.

Faithful transfer nevertheless has a limited interpretation. A correctly transmitted instruction may still propose an unsuitable experiment or rest on weak scientific assumptions. Accordingly, the study will evaluate whether handoffs preserve the supplied plan, without treating preservation as evidence that the plan deserves execution.

## Related Work

Agent Workflow Memory describes extracting reusable workflows from agent trajectories and supplying selected workflows during later action generation [S1]. Its authors study web navigation on Mind2Web and WebArena. This provides an analogy for storing a reusable handoff procedure, such as extracting dependencies before compressing a plan. It does not establish that such procedures improve research handoffs or transfer safely across contexts. The proposed work will use a fixed conversion procedure rather than replicate the original memory system.

A-Mem organizes memories as interconnected notes with contextual descriptions, keywords, tags and links; new information can also change existing descriptions [S2]. These features motivate representing a handoff as connected records rather than an undifferentiated paragraph. An action could link to its prerequisite, authorization statement and unresolved question. However, the supplied evidence does not show that linked notes preserve permission boundaries. This remains an empirical question for the proposed study.

Chain-of-Verification separates drafting, verification-question planning, independent question answering and final revision [S3]. Its authors report reduced hallucination across their evaluated factual tasks. This motivates checking handoff claims against the source plan through separately answered questions. Permission interpretation and dependency preservation differ from factual question answering, so the reported findings cannot establish effectiveness here. Together, these sources support design choices for a testable adaptation, without demonstrating its novelty or performance.

## Methodology

The proposed conversion pipeline will begin by extracting action records from a research plan. Each record will identify the intended action, triggering condition, prerequisites, explicit permission or restriction, current completion status and expected output. Missing information will remain marked as unspecified. An intention to perform an action will not itself be recorded as permission to execute it.

The pipeline will then connect records through dependencies. For example, obtaining an evaluation result may precede selecting a configuration, while approval may be required before releasing an artifact. Links will retain the relevant source passage so that compression can be checked against the plan. Following the contextual-note inspiration of A-Mem [S2], later updates will identify which conditions or statuses changed instead of silently replacing earlier information.

A drafting stage will produce a compact handoff containing the research objective, completed work, next eligible actions and unresolved dependencies. A reusable extraction checklist, motivated by workflow reuse [S1], will guide conversion. Its applicability will remain limited to the supplied plan; previously permitted actions will not become general permissions for future tasks.

Finally, a verification stage will generate questions about whether each action retains its conditions, whether permission claims have explicit support and whether pending work has been misrepresented as complete. Following CoVe’s separation of stages [S3], questions will be answered from the source plan without showing the draft’s proposed answers. Revision will reconcile discrepancies against that evidence. Unresolved ambiguity will remain visible rather than be converted into authorization. The resulting handoff will distinguish readiness under the plan from scientific justification for the action.

## Planned Evaluation

This section presents a future evaluation plan; no experiments have been conducted. A bounded collection of research-plan scenarios will contain explicit prerequisites, permission restrictions, pending decisions and completion states. Paired variants will change one consequential condition, such as whether approval has been granted, to test whether handoffs respond to that change.

Four procedures will be compared: direct prose summarization; structured extraction without verification; prose drafting with independent verification; and the combined pipeline. They will use the same source plans, model settings and maximum output length. Repeated generations will help characterize variability, while paired comparisons will isolate differences between procedures.

Human annotators will first create a source-grounded inventory of conditions, permissions, restrictions and task states. Disagreements about ambiguous language will be recorded and adjudicated. Primary measures will be the proportion of relevant conditions omitted and the proportion of actionable handoff statements asserting unsupported permission. Restrictions lost through paraphrase will also be examined.

Task continuity will be evaluated by giving a receiving agent only the handoff and asking it to propose its next step without executing external actions. Reviewers will assess dependency violations, unnecessary repetition of completed work, unsupported completion claims and failure to surface unresolved requirements. Handoff length and reviewer effort will provide practical context for accuracy differences.

Reviewers will be blinded to conversion procedure where feasible. Results will include uncertainty estimates and separate analyses of explicit and ambiguous plans. A supplementary assessment will examine whether handoffs preserve qualifications about scientific adequacy. Even perfect continuity scores would establish only faithful continuation under the supplied plan, not that the proposed research action is scientifically appropriate.

## Limitations and Conclusion

The proposed study will test whether structured extraction and independent verification improve the transfer of conditions and permissions between research agents. Its contribution would be an evaluated conversion procedure and a source-grounded framework for measuring handoff failures. Limitations include reliance on constructed scenarios, interpretive annotation and simulated continuations. The supplied literature motivates the design but does not validate its transfer to this setting. Any eventual findings will therefore be bounded by the tested plans and agents, with handoff fidelity kept distinct from scientific soundness.

Explicit Conditions and Permissions in Research-Agent Handoffs

## Abstract

This proposal investigates how research plans can be converted into handoff notes that preserve conditions, permissions and task continuity. The research question is whether a structured, independently checked handoff reduces omitted prerequisites and unsupported authorization compared with direct summarization. Inspired by workflow reuse, contextual memory organization and draft verification [S1]–[S3], the proposed method separates intended actions from their triggering conditions, permission boundaries and unresolved dependencies. A controlled evaluation will compare four conversion procedures using supplied plans and simulated continuations. Outcomes will include missing conditions, unjustified permissions and continuity errors. The study will assess faithful transfer of a plan, while treating the scientific appropriateness of its proposed actions as a separate question.

## Introduction

A research-agent handoff must communicate more than the next task. It must preserve when an action is applicable, which prerequisites remain unmet, what authorization exists and where uncertainty requires further checking. A concise note can retain an action while dropping the qualification that makes it permissible or meaningful. For example, a plan might allow an experiment only after a dataset’s suitability has been reviewed. A handoff that simply directs the receiving agent to run the experiment would alter the plan.

The proposed study asks: which conversion procedure best preserves conditional and permission-related meaning while enabling another agent to continue the task? It will compare ordinary summarization with structured extraction, verification and their combination. The central hypothesis is that explicit representation makes omissions easier to detect, while a separate checking pass can identify unsupported additions.

Faithful transfer nevertheless has a limited interpretation. A correctly transmitted instruction may still propose an unsuitable experiment or rest on weak scientific assumptions. Accordingly, the study will evaluate whether handoffs preserve the supplied plan, without treating preservation as evidence that the plan deserves execution.

## Related Work

Agent Workflow Memory describes extracting reusable workflows from agent trajectories and supplying selected workflows during later action generation [S1]. Its authors study web navigation on Mind2Web and WebArena. This provides an analogy for storing a reusable handoff procedure, such as extracting dependencies before compressing a plan. It does not establish that such procedures improve research handoffs or transfer safely across contexts. The proposed work will use a fixed conversion procedure rather than replicate the original memory system.

A-Mem organizes memories as interconnected notes with contextual descriptions, keywords, tags and links; new information can also change existing descriptions [S2]. These features motivate representing a handoff as connected records rather than an undifferentiated paragraph. An action could link to its prerequisite, authorization statement and unresolved question. However, the supplied evidence does not show that linked notes preserve permission boundaries. This remains an empirical question for the proposed study.

Chain-of-Verification separates drafting, verification-question planning, independent question answering and final revision [S3]. Its authors report reduced hallucination across their evaluated factual tasks. This motivates checking handoff claims against the source plan through separately answered questions. Permission interpretation and dependency preservation differ from factual question answering, so the reported findings cannot establish effectiveness here. Together, these sources support design choices for a testable adaptation, without demonstrating its novelty or performance.

## Methodology

The proposed conversion pipeline will begin by extracting action records from a research plan. Each record will identify the intended action, triggering condition, prerequisites, explicit permission or restriction, current completion status and expected output. Missing information will remain marked as unspecified. An intention to perform an action will not itself be recorded as permission to execute it.

The pipeline will then connect records through dependencies. For example, obtaining an evaluation result may precede selecting a configuration, while approval may be required before releasing an artifact. Links will retain the relevant source passage so that compression can be checked against the plan. Following the contextual-note inspiration of A-Mem [S2], later updates will identify which conditions or statuses changed instead of silently replacing earlier information.

A drafting stage will produce a compact handoff containing the research objective, completed work, next eligible actions and unresolved dependencies. A reusable extraction checklist, motivated by workflow reuse [S1], will guide conversion. Each application of the checklist will be limited to the supplied plan, as will any permissions recorded during conversion; previously permitted actions will not become general permissions for future tasks.

Finally, a verification stage will generate questions about whether each action retains its conditions, whether permission claims have explicit support and whether pending work has been misrepresented as complete. Following CoVe’s separation of stages [S3], questions will be answered from the source plan without showing the draft’s proposed answers. Revision will reconcile discrepancies against that evidence. Unresolved ambiguity will remain visible rather than be converted into authorization. The resulting handoff will distinguish readiness under the plan from scientific justification for the action.

## Planned Evaluation

This section presents a future evaluation plan; no experiments have been conducted. A bounded collection of research-plan scenarios will contain explicit prerequisites, permission restrictions, pending decisions and completion states. Paired variants will change one consequential condition, such as whether approval has been granted, to test whether handoffs respond to that change.

Four procedures will be compared: direct prose summarization; structured extraction without verification; prose drafting with independent verification; and the combined pipeline. They will use the same source plans, model settings and maximum output length. Repeated generations will help characterize variability, while paired comparisons will isolate differences between procedures.

Human annotators will first create a source-grounded inventory of conditions, permissions, restrictions and task states. Disagreements about ambiguous language will be recorded and adjudicated. Primary measures will be the proportion of relevant conditions omitted and the proportion of actionable handoff statements asserting unsupported permission. Restrictions lost through paraphrase will also be examined.

Task continuity will be evaluated by giving a receiving agent only the handoff and asking it to propose its next step without executing external actions. Reviewers will assess dependency violations, unnecessary repetition of completed work, unsupported completion claims and failure to surface unresolved requirements. Handoff length and reviewer effort will provide practical context for accuracy differences.

Reviewers will be blinded to conversion procedure where feasible. Results will include uncertainty estimates and separate analyses of explicit and ambiguous plans. A supplementary assessment will examine whether handoffs preserve qualifications about scientific adequacy. Even perfect continuity scores would establish only fidelity to the supplied plan, not scientific appropriateness.

## Limitations and Conclusion

The proposed study will test whether structured extraction and independent verification improve the transfer of conditions and permissions between research agents. Its contribution would be an evaluated conversion procedure and a source-grounded framework for measuring handoff failures. Limitations include reliance on constructed scenarios, interpretive annotation and simulated continuations. The supplied literature motivates the design but does not validate its transfer to this setting. Any eventual findings will therefore be bounded by the tested plans and agents, with handoff fidelity kept distinct from scientific soundness.

It must preserve when an action is applicable, which prerequisites remain unmet, what authorization exists and where uncertainty requires further checking. A concise note can retain an action while dropping the qualification that makes it permissible or meaningful. For example, a plan might allow an experiment only after a dataset’s suitability has been reviewed. A handoff that simply directs the receiving agent to run the experiment would alter the plan.

The proposed study asks: which conversion procedure best preserves conditional and permission-related meaning while enabling another agent to continue the task? It will compare ordinary summarization with structured extraction, verification and their combination. The central hypothesis is that explicit representation makes omissions easier to detect, while a separate checking pass can identify unsupported additions.

Explicit Conditions and Permissions in Research-Agent Handoffs

## Abstract

This proposal investigates how research plans can be converted into handoff notes that preserve conditions, permissions and task continuity. The research question is whether a structured, independently checked handoff reduces omitted prerequisites and unsupported authorization compared with direct summarization. Inspired by workflow reuse, contextual memory organization and draft verification [S1]–[S3], the proposed method separates intended actions from their triggering conditions, permission boundaries and unresolved dependencies. A controlled evaluation will compare four conversion procedures using supplied plans and simulated continuations. Outcomes will include missing conditions, unjustified permissions and continuity errors. The study will assess faithful transfer of a plan, while treating the scientific appropriateness of its proposed actions as a separate question.

## Introduction

A research-agent handoff must communicate more than the next task. It must preserve when an action is applicable, which prerequisites remain unmet, what authorization exists and where uncertainty requires further checking. A concise note can retain an action while dropping the qualification that makes it permissible or meaningful. For example, a plan might allow an experiment only after a dataset’s suitability has been reviewed. A handoff that simply directs the receiving agent to run the experiment would alter the plan.

The proposed study asks: which conversion procedure best preserves conditional and permission-related meaning while enabling another agent to continue the task? It will compare ordinary summarization with structured extraction, verification and their combination. The central hypothesis is that explicit representation makes omissions easier to detect, while a separate checking pass can identify unsupported additions.

Faithful transfer nevertheless has a limited interpretation. A correctly transmitted instruction may still propose an unsuitable experiment or rest on weak scientific assumptions. Accordingly, the study will evaluate whether handoffs preserve the supplied plan, without treating preservation as evidence that the plan deserves execution.

## Related Work

Agent Workflow Memory describes extracting reusable workflows from agent trajectories and supplying selected workflows during later action generation [S1]. Its authors study web navigation on Mind2Web and WebArena. This provides an analogy for storing a reusable handoff procedure, such as extracting dependencies before compressing a plan. It does not establish that such procedures improve research handoffs or transfer safely across contexts. The proposed work will use a fixed conversion procedure rather than replicate the original memory system.

A-Mem organizes memories as interconnected notes with contextual descriptions, keywords, tags and links; new information can also change existing descriptions [S2]. These features motivate representing a handoff as connected records rather than an undifferentiated paragraph. An action could link to its prerequisite, authorization statement and unresolved question. However, the supplied evidence does not show that linked notes preserve permission boundaries. This remains an empirical question for the proposed study.

Chain-of-Verification separates drafting, verification-question planning, independent question answering and final revision [S3]. Its authors report reduced hallucination across their evaluated factual tasks. This motivates checking handoff claims against the source plan through separately answered questions. Permission interpretation and dependency preservation differ from factual question answering, so the reported findings cannot establish effectiveness here. Together, these sources support design choices for a testable adaptation, without demonstrating its novelty or performance.

## Methodology

The proposed conversion pipeline will begin by extracting action records from a research plan. Each record will identify the intended action, triggering condition, prerequisites, explicit permission or restriction, current completion status and expected output. Missing information will remain marked as unspecified. An intention to perform an action will not itself be recorded as permission to execute it.

The pipeline will then connect records through dependencies. For example, obtaining an evaluation result may precede selecting a configuration, while approval may be required before releasing an artifact. Links will retain the relevant source passage so that compression can be checked against the plan. Following the contextual-note inspiration of A-Mem [S2], later updates will identify which conditions or statuses changed instead of silently replacing earlier information.

A drafting stage will produce a compact handoff containing the research objective, completed work, next eligible actions and unresolved dependencies. A reusable extraction checklist, motivated by workflow reuse [S1], will guide conversion. Its applicability will remain limited to the supplied plan; previously permitted actions will not become general permissions for future tasks.

Finally, a verification stage will generate questions about whether each action retains its conditions, whether permission claims have explicit support and whether pending work has been misrepresented as complete. Following CoVe’s separation of stages [S3], questions will be answered from the source plan without showing the draft’s proposed answers. Revision will reconcile discrepancies against that evidence. Unresolved ambiguity will remain visible rather than be converted into authorization. The resulting handoff will distinguish readiness under the plan from scientific justification for the action.

## Planned Evaluation

This section presents a future evaluation plan; no experiments have been conducted. A bounded collection of research-plan scenarios will contain explicit prerequisites, permission restrictions, pending decisions and completion states. Paired variants will change one consequential condition, such as whether approval has been granted, to test whether handoffs respond to that change.

Four procedures will be compared: direct prose summarization; structured extraction without verification; prose drafting with independent verification; and the combined pipeline. They will use the same source plans, model settings and maximum output length. Repeated generations will help characterize variability, while paired comparisons will isolate differences between procedures.

Human annotators will first create a source-grounded inventory of conditions, permissions, restrictions and task states. Disagreements about ambiguous language will be recorded and adjudicated. Primary measures will be the proportion of relevant conditions omitted and the proportion of actionable handoff statements asserting unsupported permission. Restrictions lost through paraphrase will also be examined.

Task continuity will be evaluated by giving a receiving agent only the handoff and asking it to propose its next step without executing external actions. Reviewers will assess dependency violations, unnecessary repetition of completed work, unsupported completion claims and failure to surface unresolved requirements. Handoff length and reviewer effort will provide practical context for accuracy differences.

Reviewers will be blinded to conversion procedure where feasible. Results will include uncertainty estimates and separate analyses of explicit and ambiguous plans. A supplementary assessment will examine whether handoffs preserve qualifications about scientific adequacy. Even perfect continuity scores would establish only faithful continuation under the supplied plan, not that the proposed research action is scientifically appropriate.

## Limitations and Conclusion

The proposed study will test whether structured extraction and independent verification improve the transfer of conditions and permissions between research agents. Its contribution would be an evaluated conversion procedure and a source-grounded framework for measuring handoff failures. Limitations include reliance on constructed scenarios, interpretive annotation and simulated continuations. The supplied literature motivates the design but does not validate its transfer to this setting. Any eventual findings will therefore be bounded by the tested plans and agents, with handoff fidelity kept distinct from scientific soundness.

Inspired by workflow reuse, contextual memory organization and draft verification [S1]–[S3], the proposed method separates intended actions from their triggering conditions, permission boundaries and unresolved dependencies. A controlled evaluation will compare four conversion procedures using supplied plans and simulated continuations. Outcomes will include missing conditions, unjustified permissions and continuity errors. The study will assess faithful transfer of a plan, while treating the scientific appropriateness of its proposed actions as a separate question.

## Introduction

A research-agent handoff must communicate more than the next task. It must preserve when an action is applicable, which prerequisites remain unmet, what authorization exists and where uncertainty requires further checking. A concise note can retain an action while dropping the qualification that makes it permissible or meaningful. For example, a plan might allow an experiment only after a dataset’s suitability has been reviewed. A handoff that simply directs the receiving agent to run the experiment would alter the plan.

The proposed study asks: which conversion procedure best preserves conditional and permission-related meaning while enabling another agent to continue the task? It will compare ordinary summarization with structured extraction, verification and their combination. The central hypothesis is that explicit representation makes omissions easier to detect, while a separate checking pass can identify unsupported additions.

Faithful transfer nevertheless has a limited interpretation. A correctly transmitted instruction may still propose an unsuitable experiment or rest on weak scientific assumptions. Accordingly, the study will evaluate whether handoffs preserve the supplied plan, without treating preservation as evidence that the plan deserves execution.

## Related Work

Agent Workflow Memory describes extracting reusable workflows from agent trajectories and supplying selected workflows during later action generation [S1]. Its authors study web navigation on Mind2Web and WebArena. This provides an analogy for storing a reusable handoff procedure, such as extracting dependencies before compressing a plan. It does not establish that such procedures improve research handoffs or transfer safely across contexts. The proposed work will use a fixed conversion procedure rather than replicate the original memory system.

A-Mem organizes memories as interconnected notes with contextual descriptions, keywords, tags and links; new information can also change existing descriptions [S2]. These features motivate representing a handoff as connected records rather than an undifferentiated paragraph. An action could link to its prerequisite, authorization statement and unresolved question. However, the supplied evidence does not show that linked notes preserve permission boundaries. This remains an empirical question for the proposed study.

Chain-of-Verification separates drafting, verification-question planning, independent question answering and final revision [S3]. Its authors report reduced hallucination across their evaluated factual tasks. This motivates checking handoff claims against the source plan through separately answered questions. Permission interpretation and dependency preservation differ from factual question answering, so the reported findings cannot establish effectiveness here. Together, these sources support design choices for a testable adaptation, without demonstrating its novelty or performance.

## Methodology

The proposed conversion pipeline will begin by extracting action records from a research plan. Each record will identify the intended action, triggering condition, prerequisites, explicit permission or restriction, current completion status and expected output. Missing information will remain marked as unspecified. An intention to perform an action will not itself be recorded as permission to execute it.

The pipeline will then connect records through dependencies. For example, obtaining an evaluation result may precede selecting a configuration, while approval may be required before releasing an artifact. Links will retain the relevant source passage so that compression can be checked against the plan. Following the contextual-note inspiration of A-Mem [S2], later updates will identify which conditions or statuses changed instead of silently replacing earlier information.

A drafting stage will produce a compact handoff containing the research objective, completed work, next eligible actions and unresolved dependencies. A reusable extraction checklist, motivated by workflow reuse [S1], will guide conversion. In each conversion, the checklist will apply only to the supplied plan; previously permitted actions will not become general permissions for future tasks.

Finally, a verification stage will generate questions about whether each action retains its conditions, whether permission claims have explicit support and whether pending work has been misrepresented as complete. Following CoVe’s separation of stages [S3], questions will be answered from the source plan without showing the draft’s proposed answers. Revision will reconcile discrepancies against that evidence. Unresolved ambiguity will remain visible rather than be converted into authorization. The resulting handoff will distinguish readiness under the plan from scientific justification for the action.

## Planned Evaluation

This section presents a future evaluation plan; no experiments have been conducted. A bounded collection of research-plan scenarios will contain explicit prerequisites, permission restrictions, pending decisions and completion states. Paired variants will change one consequential condition, such as whether approval has been granted, to test whether handoffs respond to that change.

Four procedures will be compared: direct prose summarization; structured extraction without verification; prose drafting with independent verification; and the combined pipeline. They will use the same source plans, model settings and maximum output length. Repeated generations will help characterize variability, while paired comparisons will isolate differences between procedures.

Human annotators will first create a source-grounded inventory of conditions, permissions, restrictions and task states. Disagreements about ambiguous language will be recorded and adjudicated. Primary measures will be the proportion of relevant conditions omitted and the proportion of actionable handoff statements asserting unsupported permission. Restrictions lost through paraphrase will also be examined.

Task continuity will be evaluated by giving a receiving agent only the handoff and asking it to propose its next step without executing external actions. Reviewers will assess dependency violations, unnecessary repetition of completed work, unsupported completion claims and failure to surface unresolved requirements. Handoff length and reviewer effort will provide practical context for accuracy differences.

Reviewers will be blinded to conversion procedure where feasible. Results will include uncertainty estimates and separate analyses of explicit and ambiguous plans. A supplementary assessment will examine whether handoffs preserve qualifications about scientific adequacy. Even perfect continuity scores would establish only faithful continuation under the supplied plan, not that the proposed research action is scientifically appropriate.

## Limitations and Conclusion

The proposed study will test whether structured extraction and independent verification improve the transfer of conditions and permissions between research agents. Its contribution would be an evaluated conversion procedure and a source-grounded framework for measuring handoff failures. Limitations include reliance on constructed scenarios, interpretive annotation and simulated continuations. The supplied literature motivates the design but does not validate its transfer to this setting. Any eventual findings will therefore be bounded by the tested plans and agents, with handoff fidelity kept distinct from scientific soundness.

Explicit Conditions and Permissions in Research-Agent Handoffs

## Abstract

This proposal investigates how research plans can be converted into handoff notes that preserve conditions, permissions and task continuity. The research question is whether a structured, independently checked handoff reduces omitted prerequisites and unsupported authorization compared with direct summarization. Inspired by workflow reuse, contextual memory organization and draft verification [S1]–[S3], the proposed method separates intended actions from their triggering conditions, permission boundaries and unresolved dependencies. A controlled evaluation will compare four conversion procedures using supplied plans and simulated continuations. Outcomes will include missing conditions, unjustified permissions and continuity errors. The study will assess faithful transfer of a plan, while treating the scientific appropriateness of its proposed actions as a separate question.

## Introduction

A research-agent handoff must communicate more than the next task. It must preserve when an action is applicable, which prerequisites remain unmet, what authorization exists and where uncertainty requires further checking. A concise note can retain an action while dropping the qualification that makes it permissible or meaningful. For example, a plan might allow an experiment only after a dataset’s suitability has been reviewed. A handoff that simply directs the receiving agent to run the experiment would alter the plan.

The proposed study asks: which conversion procedure best preserves conditional and permission-related meaning while enabling another agent to continue the task? It will compare ordinary summarization with structured extraction, verification and their combination. The central hypothesis is that explicit representation makes omissions easier to detect, while a separate checking pass can identify unsupported additions.

Faithful transfer nevertheless has a limited interpretation. A correctly transmitted instruction may still propose an unsuitable experiment or rest on weak scientific assumptions. Accordingly, the study will evaluate whether handoffs preserve the supplied plan, without treating preservation as evidence that the plan deserves execution.

## Related Work

Agent Workflow Memory describes extracting reusable workflows from agent trajectories and supplying selected workflows during later action generation [S1]. Its authors study web navigation on Mind2Web and WebArena. This provides an analogy for storing a reusable handoff procedure, such as extracting dependencies before compressing a plan. It does not establish that such procedures improve research handoffs or transfer safely across contexts. The proposed work will use a fixed conversion procedure rather than replicate the original memory system.

A-Mem organizes memories as interconnected notes with contextual descriptions, keywords, tags and links; new information can also change existing descriptions [S2]. These features motivate representing a handoff as connected records rather than an undifferentiated paragraph. An action could link to its prerequisite, authorization statement and unresolved question. However, the supplied evidence does not show that linked notes preserve permission boundaries. This remains an empirical question for the proposed study.

Chain-of-Verification separates drafting, verification-question planning, independent question answering and final revision [S3]. Its authors report reduced hallucination across their evaluated factual tasks. This motivates checking handoff claims against the source plan through separately answered questions. Permission interpretation and dependency preservation differ from factual question answering, so the reported findings cannot establish effectiveness here. Together, these sources support design choices for a testable adaptation, without demonstrating its novelty or performance.

## Methodology

The proposed conversion pipeline will begin by extracting action records from a research plan. Each record will identify the intended action, triggering condition, prerequisites, explicit permission or restriction, current completion status and expected output. Missing information will remain marked as unspecified. An intention to perform an action will not itself be recorded as permission to execute it.

The pipeline will then connect records through dependencies. For example, obtaining an evaluation result may precede selecting a configuration, while approval may be required before releasing an artifact. Links will retain the relevant source passage so that compression can be checked against the plan. Following the contextual-note inspiration of A-Mem [S2], later updates will identify which conditions or statuses changed instead of silently replacing earlier information.

A drafting stage will produce a compact handoff containing the research objective, completed work, next eligible actions and unresolved dependencies. A reusable extraction checklist, motivated by workflow reuse [S1], will guide conversion. Its applicability will remain limited to the supplied plan; previously permitted actions will not become general permissions for future tasks.

Finally, a verification stage will generate questions about whether each action retains its conditions, whether permission claims have explicit support and whether pending work has been misrepresented as complete. Following CoVe’s separation of stages [S3], questions will be answered from the source plan without showing the draft’s proposed answers. Revision will reconcile discrepancies against that evidence. Unresolved ambiguity will remain visible rather than be converted into authorization. The resulting handoff will distinguish readiness under the plan from scientific justification for the action.

## Planned Evaluation

This section presents a future evaluation plan; no experiments have been conducted. A bounded collection of research-plan scenarios will contain explicit prerequisites, permission restrictions, pending decisions and completion states. Paired variants will change one consequential condition, such as whether approval has been granted, to test whether handoffs respond to that change.

Four procedures will be compared: direct prose summarization; structured extraction without verification; prose drafting with independent verification; and the combined pipeline. They will use the same source plans, model settings and maximum output length. Repeated generations will help characterize variability, while paired comparisons will isolate differences between procedures.

Human annotators will first create a source-grounded inventory of conditions, permissions, restrictions and task states. Disagreements about ambiguous language will be recorded and adjudicated. Primary measures will be the proportion of relevant conditions omitted and the proportion of actionable handoff statements asserting unsupported permission. Restrictions lost through paraphrase will also be examined.

Task continuity will be evaluated by giving a receiving agent only the handoff and asking it to propose its next step without executing external actions. Reviewers will assess dependency violations, unnecessary repetition of completed work, unsupported completion claims and failure to surface unresolved requirements. Handoff length and reviewer effort will provide practical context for accuracy differences.

Reviewers will be blinded to conversion procedure where feasible. Results will include uncertainty estimates and separate analyses of explicit and ambiguous plans. A supplementary assessment will examine whether handoffs preserve qualifications about scientific adequacy. Even perfect continuity scores would establish only faithful continuation under the supplied plan, not that the proposed research action is scientifically appropriate.

## Limitations and Conclusion

The proposed study will test whether structured extraction and independent verification improve the transfer of conditions and permissions between research agents. Its contribution would be an evaluated conversion procedure and a source-grounded framework for measuring handoff failures. Limitations include reliance on constructed scenarios, interpretive annotation and simulated continuations. The supplied literature motivates the design but does not validate its transfer to this setting. Any eventual findings will therefore be bounded by the tested plans and agents, with handoff fidelity kept distinct from scientific soundness.
